pages.text: Inside the vault that holds the lost treasures of Pompeii | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE Inside the vault that holds the lost treasures of Pompeii From vintage wine to restored frescoes, National Geographic gained access to thousands of fragile artifacts that capture the customs and joys of ancient Roman life. National Geographic gained access to the thousands of fragile archaeological objects from Pompeii and Herculaneum kept in the museum's secluded storerooms. By Rose Minutaglio Photographs by Paolo Verzone Video by Massimo Nicolaci Published July 27, 2026 In 1709, an Italian farmer digging a well beneath the town of Ercolano struck something strange: a slab of stage from an opulent Roman theater, once the pride of a luxurious seaside getaway called Herculaneum. When Mount Vesuvius erupted in A.D. 79, the town was entombed under 60 feet of volcanic rock—and erased from memory. The farmer’s discovery set off a treasure hunt. Charles of Bourbon, the 18th century king of Naples, ordered systematic excavations. Bronze and marble statues were hauled off, along with gold bracelets, jeweled rings, amphorae, and coins—even an intact boat was uncovered. Some of the bounty was plundered, but a lot of it survived. Today much of that royal excavation, alongside other priceless artifacts from Herculaneum’s sister city of Pompeii, resides at Italy’s National Archaeological Museum of Naples, a grand 16th-century building in the heart of the city. Courtship behavior among insects has as much drama as you see among bigger creatures. Turkeys take a puffed-up strut around their territories. Bullfrogs bellow to one another in baritone. You may be aware of the various ways large animals signal that they’re ready for love. But what about all the little animals? After all, beetles, spiders, and flies have to find partners too. And just because the stage is smaller does not mean there’s any less drama. Developed under the auspices of the NIST Coatings Service Life Prediction Consortium, the NIST 2 m integrating sphere provides a source of collimated ultraviolet radiation in the 290 nm to 400 nm region of the spectrum. Visible and infrared components of the input radiation are largely removed by dichroic mirrors or filters. The physics of integrating spheres ensures that the uniformity of the UV radiation emitted from a sphere exit aperture is ³ 95%. By coupling the integrating sphere with a high intensity UV light source, irradiance levels equivalent to 60 or more "suns" can be achieved at the sphere exit apertures. The exit apertures in the sphere can be connected to specimen chambers, with the specific type of chamber utilized being dependent on the material being tested. pages.description: The crustaceans, non-native and fierce, are taking over the Gulf of Maine. Could eating them help draw down the population?
pages.text: Invasive green crabs: If you can't beat them, eat them. | National Geographic By Kea Krause Photographs by Brian Skerry Published July 11, 2022 • 12 min read West Bath, Maine — If you close your eyes, a green crab scuttling up your forearm feels more spider than sea creature, its little legs picking their way as if spinning silk. If you open your eyes, you will see the forged work of 200 million years: bumpy carapace, plated apron, calcified pincers. The small crabs are exquisite, seemingly carved from jade. The big ones are monstrous looking. They are nimble and chaotic, and likely under any beach rock in the Gulf of Maine. But here, the European green crab is not native. It is an invader , a species that traveled to the region in the 1800s in the ballast water of trading ships. In the centuries since, the crabs have established a thriving population, feasting on soft-shell clams and blue mussels, overtaking fisheries that have sustained Mainers for centuries. Their monstrous appetites and canny ability to adapt and reproduce have outcompeted any efforts to remove them. Green crabs ( Carcinus maenas ) are an invasive species that first appeared in New England waters in the 1800s, mostly likely arriving in the onboard water of large oceangoing vessels. The species’ population has exploded in recent years due to warming seawater temperatures in the Gulf of Maine. Now, one of the last defenses against these marauding creatures is not to eradicate them, but to eat them . On its back, an overlapping fan of stiff structures likely caught the light, vibrant with color. pages.text: Itemized deductions, standard deduction | Internal Revenue Service Skip to main content Itemized deductions, standard deduction More In Help Interactive Tax Assistant Tools Report fraud Tax scams Identity theft Notices and letters Appeals Frequently asked questions Accessibility Contact your local IRS office Contact an international IRS office Tax topics Other languages Top Frequently Asked Questions for Itemized Deductions, Standard Deduction If I must deduct points over the life of my mortgage, and I have a 30-year mortgage, should I divide the points paid by 30 and enter that amount on Schedule A of Form 1040? Answer: No. While you must deduct the points over the life of the loan ratably (equally), you don't divide the points by 30 years. Instead, you divide the points by the number of payments scheduled over the term of the loan (360 monthly payments in the case of a 30-year mortgage) and deduct points each year according to the number of payments you made in that year (less than twelve payments in some cases). If the loan ends prematurely, for example, because you paid it off or refinanced with a different lender, then the remaining points are deductible in that year. Note: This does not apply to loans refinanced with the same lender. Any deductible points not included on Form 1098 (usually not included on the Form when refinancing) should be entered on Schedule A (Form 1040), Itemized Deductions , line 8c "Points not reported to you on Form 1098." Whenever the whistle blew, the Wales flanker in the red scrum cap took an age to rise. Precious seconds to recover. Nobody counts tackles when the ball is dead. But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up. By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed. Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight. Jeffrey Novak Principal Deputy General Counsel Novak was appointed Principal Deputy General Counsel in May 2025 and served as Acting General Counsel until October 2025. He is an Honors College graduate of Ball State University and a graduate of the Indiana University School of Law. During law school, Novak worked as a law clerk for Bill Cummings, formerly the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. After graduating law school, he served a two-year clerkship with the late Charles R. Richey, United States District Judge for the District of Columbia, before joining McGuire Woods, where he was elected to partnership. Before joining the Department, he worked in a variety of roles at technology companies over the course of more than 20 years, including managing litigation, compliance, patent, and public policy functions, while also serving on the boards of the Northern Virginia Technology Council, the Internet Association, and the Virginia Early Childhood Foundation.

In this position, he is responsible for the full range of human capital services covering DOE's workforce of 13,000 Federal employees. Working with the Chief Human Capital Officer, he sets strategic direction and programmatic priorities for the human capital organization and provides leadership across a myriad of teams responsible for DOE workforce planning, advisory services, hiring, benefits, policy, employee and labor relations, executive resources management, talent management, engagement, human resources information technology, and accountability. He provides oversight to shared service centers supporting DOE Headquarters, national program offices, and power administrations. Jeff has over 30 years of Federal service and has been with the Department of Energy since 2009. Jeff has served in various senior leadership positions within Human Capital to include four Shared Service Centers (SSCs) and the Office of Business Operations. The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026. It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran. Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter." Close jfd553's Diary Mapping Icefields Parkway, Part 1: A two-year mapping journey Posted by jfd553 on 4 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 6 November 2026. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. Included below are a few snapshots taken in the field, which capture the majestic landscapes along the Icefields Parkway. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. The parkway offers exceptional alpine landscape, with glaciers, rivers, turquoise lakes, and breathtaking mountain views directly from the roadside (Figure 1). Best of all, many of these landmarks can be reached in a single day’s hike (Figure 2). Figure 1: North Saskatchewan River alongside the parkway. The funds are used to hire dedicated staff that provide individualized career and training-related services to eligible veterans and eligible persons with employment barriers, and to assist employers in filling their workforce needs with job-seeking veterans.
